'''Yugasan Rendaiji''' ({{ill|rendaiji|ja|蓮台寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rendaiji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11621648}}) is a temple of the {{ill|Shingon Omuro School|ja|真言宗御室派|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingon Mimuro Sect|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q420739}} located in the Kojima area of {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|qid=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki City}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|qid=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}. It is classified as an Extraordinary Head Temple. Its mountain name is Yuka-yama (由加山), and its principal images are the Eleven-faced Kannon Bosatsu and Yogācāra Daigongen. It is pilgrimage site No. 6 on the {{ill|Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage|qid=Q987974|lt=China 33 Kannon Pilgrimage}} and No. 8 on the {{ill|Hyakuhachi Kannon Pilgrimage|ja|百八観音霊場|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyakuhachi Kannon Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.

== History ==
Tradition holds that in the 10th year of the {{ill|Tenpyō|en|Tenpyō|qid=Q1199879|lt=Tenpyō Era}} (738), the monk {{ill|Gyōki|en|Gyōki|qid=Q1136664|lt=Gyōki}} enshrined the Eleven-faced Kannon Bosatsu (the principal image) along with Yogācāra Daigongen (a manifestation of the trace of Amida and Yakushi) and thus founded the temple. Although the temple declined after being damaged by warfare at the end of the Heian period, it was revived during the Muromachi period by a high-Ranking monk. In the Edo period it received the protection of the {{ill|Okayama Domain|en|Okayama Domain|qid=Q903497|lt=Okayama Han}} of Bizen Province. Long revered for its Yogācāra Daigongen, following the Meiji [[:en:Shinbutsu Bunri|Shinbutsu Bunri]] edict, a separate shrine – later known as {{ill|Yuga Shrine|ja|由加神社本宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuka Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11577571}} – was established within the temple grounds. 

After the post–World War II dissolution of State Shinto, although formally separated, the monastic staff continued to perform rituals in the main hall so that, in practice, the pre–Meiji state of affairs was restored. As a result, while Yuka Shrine retained its legal status as a separate religious corporation and maintained its own priests, it was in effect nearly dormant.

In 1997 (Heisei 9) on March 3, Yuka Shrine began independent religious activities by occupying part of the temple buildings. Since then Rendaiji and Yuka Shrine have been in conflict—with Rendaiji seeking the return of its buildings—though Yuka Shrine continues its independent operations.

A traditional custom called “Ryōmairi” (simultaneous pilgrimage to both shrines) developed in the Edo period in which pilgrims visited both the Yogācāra Daigongen of Yugasan and the {{ill|Konpira Gongen|ja|金毘羅大権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kinpirō Daigongen|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金毘羅権現|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q167077}} (now at {{ill|Kotohira-gū|en|Kotohira-gū|qid=Q94760|lt=Kintōhira-gū}}) in Sanuki Province.

== Overview ==
It is widely venerated as a protective deity against misfortune. In 2007 (Heisei 19) a 7.59-meter tall wooden statue of the immovable 【ill|Fudō Myōō|ja|不動明王】—the tallest of its kind in Japan—was completed.

The approach (sando) up Yuka-yama is lined by a traditional town (monzenchō) whose local specialty is the sweet rice cake known as {{ill|ankoro mochi|ja|あんころ餅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ankoro Mochi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11258809}}.

== Cultural Properties ==
; Okayama Prefecture–designated Important Cultural Properties
* The Nakazato Fujizuka (mound) – one of the fujizuka built by the Fuji-kō group (pilgrims to Mt. Fuji) from the Edo period to early Showa period. In Kurashiki it is one of the larger mounds, with a height of 12 meters from its southern base and a diameter of 30 meters. A stone monument dated to 1822 (Bunsei 5) indicates that its construction began in the Edo period. Among 36 stone structures, its dōsojin monument is unique in the district.
; Treasures
* Ema (votive plaques) depicting the subjugation of the Yamata no Orochi (dating from Tenpō 5, July)
* Ema commemorating a Fuji ascent (dating from Keien 7, June)
* Ema depicting a pilgrimage to Ise (by Fujigoro and Murata Masatarō, dating from Keien 3, March)＜ref＞{{Cite book|和書|author=Ishikamin Library Local Materials Section|title=Ema of Nerima|publisher=Nerima City Board of Education|year=1978|page=175,178}}＜/ref＞
== Address ==
* 2855 Kojima Yuka, Kurashiki City, Okayama Prefecture
== Access ==
* By car: From the {{ill|Seto-Chūō Expressway|en|Seto-Chūō Expressway|qid=Q11566530|lt=Setchu Chūō Expressway}} at {{ill|Mizushima interchange|ja|水島IC|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizushima IC|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 水島インターチェンジ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11129865}}, take {{ill|Okayama Prefectural Road Route 21|ja|岡山児島線|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okayama Kojima Road No.21|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 岡山県道21号岡山児島線|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11472422}} east toward Okayama, and at the “Gōnai” intersection turn east onto {{ill|Okayama Prefectural Road Route 62|ja|玉野福田線|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okayama Tamano Fukuda Line|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 岡山県道62号玉野福田線|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11472679}}. Continue straight along the route – about 15 minutes by car.
* By train: Approximately a 15-minute taxi ride from {{ill|Kojima Station|en|Kojima Station|qid=Q4981057|lt=Kojima Station}} on the {{ill|Seto-Ōhashi Line|en|Seto-Ōhashi Line|qid=Q7456750|lt=Seto Ohashi Line}}.
* By bus: A “Shimoden” bus (downward bus) runs from Kojima Station; however, there are only two round-trips per day (one in the morning, one in the evening) with a stop time of about 5 minutes. (Buses do not run on Saturdays, Sundays, holidays, or the New Year’s three days.)

'''Rendaiji''' (蓮台寺) is a temple of the {{ill|Shingon Omuro School|ja|真言宗御室派|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Omuro School of Shingon Buddhism|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q420739}} in {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|qid=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|qid=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}, classified as a Special Head Temple. Its mountain name is {{ill|Yuga Mountain|ja|由加山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuga Mountain|qq=}}. The main images are {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|qid=Q11404731|lt=Eleven-Faced Kannon}} and {{ill|Yuga Daigongen|ja|瑜伽大権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuga Daigongen|qq=}}. It is the 6th temple in the {{ill|Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage|qid=Q987974|lt=Chūgoku 33 Kannon Pilgrimage}} and the 8th in the {{ill|108 Kannon Pilgrimage|ja|百八観音霊場|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/108 Kannon Pilgrimage|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.

== History ==
According to tradition, Rendaiji was founded in {{ill|738|en|738|qid=Q23585|lt=738 CE}} (Tenpyō 10) by {{ill|Gyōki|en|Gyōki|qid=Q1136664|lt=Gyōki}}, who enshrined Eleven-Faced Kannon as the main deity alongside {{ill|Yuga Daigongen|ja|瑜伽大権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuga Daigongen|qq=}}, manifestations of {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|qid=Q236242|lt=Amitābha}} and {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|Bhaisajyaguru|qid=Q854773|lt=Yakushi Nyorai Medicine Buddha}}.<ref>[https://www.yugasan.jp/engi.html History of Yuga-san Rendaiji]</ref> The temple declined after being ravaged by fire in the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}}, but it was restored during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi Period}} by the monk Zōun.

During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo Period}}, it was under the protection of the {{ill|Okayama Domain|en|Okayama Domain|qid=Q903497|lt=Okayama Domain}} in {{ill|Bizen Province|en|Bizen Province|qid=Q1053688|lt=Bizen Province}}. {{ill|Yuga Daigongen|ja|瑜伽大権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuga Daigongen|qq=}} had been a focal point of faith for centuries, but the temple was divided following the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|qid=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu Bunri}} policy of the early {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治初年|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji Period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3125096}}, with the grounds allocated to form {{ill|Yuga Shrine|ja|由加神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuga Shrine|qq=}} (later Yuga Shrine Main Shrine).

After {{ill|World War II|en|World War II|qid=Q362|lt=World War II}} and the dissolution of State Shinto, the temple and shrine operated de facto as a single entity, although formally separate. In {{ill|1997|en|1997|qid=Q2088|lt=1997}} (Heisei 9), disputes arose when Yuga Shrine resumed independent religious activities, leading to a legal battle over property rights. These conflicts were attributed to disagreements between the head priest of Rendaiji and his brother, the chief priest of Yuga Shrine.

The custom of {{ill|Ryōmairi|ja|両参り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryōmairi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—visiting both Yuga Daigongen and {{ill|Kotohira-gū|lt=Konpira Daigongen|ja|金毘羅大権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotohira-gū|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 金毘羅権現}} (present-day {{ill|Kotohira-gū|en|Kotohira-gū|qid=Q94760|lt=Kotohira-gū}} in {{ill|Sanuki Province|en|Sanuki Province|qid=Q929682|lt=Sanuki Province}})—was popular during the Edo Period.

== Overview ==
Rendaiji is revered as a temple for warding off misfortunes. In {{ill|2007|en|2007|qid=Q2024|lt=2007}} (Heisei 19), Japan's tallest wooden statue of {{ill|Acala|en|Acala|qid=Q337624|lt=Fudō Myōō}} at 7.59 meters was completed.<ref>[https://yugasan.jp/19nen.html Yuga-san Rendaiji - Yakuyoke Fudō]</ref>

The a11roach to Yuga Mountain is lined with a {{ill|Monzen-machi|lt=Monzen-machi|lt=Monzen-machi|ja|門前町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Monzen-machi|qq=}}, with {{ill|ankoro mochi|ja|あんころ餅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/ankoro mochi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11258809}} as its specialty.
